questions.text: The liberalization of the Indian economy in 1991 led to which of the following fiscal outcomes?

options.text: Sharp increase in Government control over pricing
Lowering of direct and indirect tax rates

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Lowering of direct and indirect tax rates.

Key Points

  • The liberalization of the Indian economy in 1991 introduced significant fiscal reforms, primarily focusing on the reduction of tax rates to encourage compliance and broaden the tax base. Hence, the statement regarding the lowering of direct and indirect tax rates is correct.
  • Tax reforms initiated after 1991 were based on the recommendations of the Tax Reforms Committee, also known as the Raja Chelliah Committee, which suggested reducing the high rates of Personal Income Tax and Corporate Tax.
  • In terms of Indirect Taxes, there was a drastic reduction in Customs Duties (import duties) to make the Indian economy more integrated with the global market. Peak customs duty rates were reduced from over 200% in 1991 to much lower levels in subsequent years.
  • The reforms aimed at simplifying the tax structure and removing the complexities of the Excise Duty system, eventually leading to the implementation of MODVAT (Modified Value Added Tax) and later CENVAT.
  • While liberalization aimed at fiscal discipline, it did not lead to the elimination of all public debt; in fact, managing fiscal deficit remained a challenge for the Government of India. Hence, the statement about the elimination of public debt is incorrect.
  • The New Economic Policy (NEP) actually decreased Government control over pricing in most sectors (except essential commodities) to allow market forces to determine prices. Hence, the statement about increased control is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • New Economic Policy (NEP) of 1991: Launched during the tenure of Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, the policy was a response to a severe Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis.
  • LPG Framework: The reforms are famously known as Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization. Liberalization referred to the end of License Raj, Privatization involved disinvestment in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), and Globalization aimed at opening the Indian economy to Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
  • Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA): To facilitate external trade and payments, the stringent Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) of 1973 was eventually replaced by the more liberal FEMA in 1999.
  • Industrial Licensing: Under the 1991 reforms, industrial licensing was abolished for almost all industries, except for a small list of 18 industries related to security, strategic concerns, and social reasons.
  • International Support: To tide over the 1991 crisis, India had to borrow from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, which came with conditions for structural adjustments and economic stabilization.

Important Points

  • Direct Tax Reforms: Before 1991, the highest marginal rate of Income Tax was very high, which led to tax evasion. Post-reforms, the rates were gradually moderated to 10%, 20%, and 30% slabs to increase revenue collection.
  • Devaluation of Rupee: As part of the fiscal and external sector reforms, the Indian Rupee was devalued twice in July 1991 to boost exports and stabilize the Balance of Payments.
  • Banking Sector Reforms: Based on the Narasimham Committee (1991) recommendations, the government reduced the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) and Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to provide more liquidity to the banking system.
  • MRTP Act: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act was amended to remove the requirement for large companies to seek prior government approval for expansion or establishment of new undertakings.

questions.text: By how much was the rupee devalued in July 1991?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 18 per cent.

Key Points

  • The Indian Rupee was devalued in July 1991 as a response to a severe Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis that threatened the nation's economic stability.
  • The devaluation was carried out in two distinct steps by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) under the leadership of Governor S. Venkitaramanan and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh.
  • On July 1, 1991, the RBI announced a downward adjustment of the rupee's value by approximately 9 per cent against major international currencies like the US Dollar and Pound Sterling.
  • Shortly after, on July 3, 1991, a second round of devaluation was implemented, reducing the value by another 10 to 11 per cent.
  • The cumulative effect of these two adjustments resulted in a total devaluation of approximately 18 per cent to 19 per cent.
  • The primary goal of this move was to make Indian exports cheaper and more competitive in the global market while making imports more expensive to curb the outflow of foreign exchange.

Additional Information

  • Context of the 1991 Crisis: India faced a monumental economic crisis in 1991 due to high fiscal deficits, rising inflation, and the impact of the Gulf War (1990-91), which led to a surge in crude oil prices.
  • Foreign Exchange Reserves: By June 1991, India’s forex reserves had depleted to about $1.2 billion, which was barely sufficient to pay for three weeks of essential imports.
  • Gold Pledging: To avoid defaulting on international debt obligations, the Government of India had to pledge its gold reserves. Approximately 47 tonnes of gold were shipped to the Bank of England and 20 tonnes to the Union Bank of Switzerland to secure emergency loans.
  • LPG Reforms: The devaluation was a precursor to the broader New Economic Policy of 1991, which introduced Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) to open up the Indian economy.
  • Historical Devaluations: India has experienced major currency devaluations previously in 1949 (linked to the British Pound) and in 1966, when the rupee was devalued by 36.5 per cent under the Indira Gandhi administration.

Important Points

  • Devaluation vs. Depreciation: Devaluation is a deliberate downward adjustment of a country's currency value by the government or central bank in a fixed exchange rate system. In contrast, depreciation occurs due to market forces of supply and demand.
  • Exchange Rate Management: Following the 1991 crisis, India moved toward a more flexible system. In 1992, the Liberalized Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) was introduced, eventually leading to a market-determined exchange rate for the current account in 1993.
  • Impact on Trade: While devaluation helps in boosting exports, it also increases the burden of external debt and the cost of imported raw materials and fuel, contributing to imported inflation.
  • Policy Shift: The July 1991 devaluation signaled the end of the "License Raj" and the beginning of market-oriented reforms led by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.

questions.text: When did the “naya paisa”, introduced with the decimal system of coinage, become paise ?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is June 1, 1964.

Key Points

  • The transition to the decimal system of coinage in India occurred through the Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955, which was brought into force on April 1, 1957. Before this, the currency followed a non-decimal system where 1 Rupee was equal to 16 Annas, and 1 Anna was equal to 4 Pice.
  • Upon the introduction of the decimal system in April 1, 1957, the Rupee was divided into 100 units. To distinguish the new unit from the old pice, the new subunit was officially designated as "Naya Paisa" (New Paisa).
  • The term "Naya Paisa" remained in official use for a period of seven years. During this time, both old and new coins circulated together until the old denominations were phased out.
  • On June 1, 1964, the Government of India decided to drop the prefix "Naya" from the currency. From this date onwards, the unit was simply called "Paisa" (plural "Paise"). Hence, the statement regarding the change on June 1, 1964, is correct.
  • The coins issued during the 1957-1964 period carried the legend "Naya Paisa" to educate the public about the decimal division of the Rupee.

Additional Information

  • Pre-Decimal System: Before 1957, the basic unit of currency was the Rupee, which was subdivided into 16 Annas. Each Anna was further divided into 4 Pice, and each Pice into 3 Pies. This meant 1 Rupee was equivalent to 192 Pies.
  • Denominations Introduced: Under the 1957 reform, the initial denominations of "Naya Paisa" were 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, and 50 naye paise. The 1 Rupee coin remained the standard unit.
  • Withdrawal of Small Coins: Over the decades, due to inflation and the rising cost of production, smaller denominations became obsolete. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) eventually withdrew coins of denomination 25 paise and below from circulation effective from June 30, 2011.
  • Legal Authority: The Government of India has the sole right to mint coins under the Coinage Act, 2011 (which replaced the older 1906 Act). The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) acts as an agent to the Central Government for the distribution and management of these coins.
  • Mints in India: Coins are currently minted at four locations owned by the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL): Mumbai, Alipore (Kolkata), Hyderabad, and Noida.

Important Points

  • April 1, 1957: This date marks the official launch of the decimal coinage system in India. This was a landmark administrative and economic reform to simplify accounting and transactions.
  • The Term "Paisa": The word Paisa is derived from the Sanskrit word 'Padamsah', which means a quarter part. Historically, the value and metal composition of the paisa have changed significantly, moving from copper and bronze to stainless steel and ferritic stainless steel in modern times.
  • Symbol of Rupee: While the subunits (paise) evolved in 1964, the Indian Rupee got its distinct symbol (₹) much later, on July 15, 2010. It was designed by Udaya Kumar Dharmalingam.
  • Demonetization Context: While the change from Naya Paisa to Paisa was a nomenclature shift, India has seen major currency reforms, including the 1978 and 2016 demonetization of high-value banknotes. However, the 1964 change was specifically focused on the decimal subunit.

questions.text: Which of the following Banks recently launched the 7th edition of knowledge summit ‘Evolve’ for MSMEs?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Axis bank.

Key Points

  • Axis bank, India’s third-largest private sector bank, officially launched the 7th edition of its premier knowledge summit for MSMEs (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises) titled ‘Evolve’.
  • The primary theme for the 7th edition of this summit was ‘Indian MSMEs: Shifting Gears for Next Level Growth’, focusing on the transition of small businesses into larger, more competitive entities.
  • The summit aimed to provide MSMEs with a platform to understand the importance of digitalization, technology adoption, and the export potential available in the global market. Hence, the mention of Axis Bank as the organizer is correct.
  • For this edition, Axis bank partnered with industry leaders such as AWS (Amazon Web Services) and Anthill Ventures to provide specialized insights into cloud computing and scaling businesses.
  • The ‘Evolve’ summit series acts as a knowledge-sharing platform where experts discuss supply chain management, financial discipline, and sustainable business practices for the MSME sector.

Additional Information

  • Understanding MSMEs in India:
    • The MSME sector is often referred to as the backbone of the Indian economy, contributing nearly 30% to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and approximately 48% to exports.
    • The classification of MSMEs was revised under the MSMED Act, 2006, effective from July 1, 2020, merging the criteria for manufacturing and service sectors based on investment and annual turnover.
    • A Micro enterprise is defined by an investment up to Rs. 1 crore and turnover up to Rs. 5 crore; a Small enterprise up to Rs. 10 crore investment and Rs. 50 crore turnover; and a Medium enterprise up to Rs. 50 crore investment and Rs. 250 crore turnover.
  • About Axis Bank:
    • Headquartered in Mumbai, Maharashtra, Axis bank began its operations in 1994 (originally incorporated in 1993 as UTI Bank).
    • The bank was renamed to Axis bank in 2007 to create a unique brand identity distinct from its promoters.
    • As of recent reports, Amitabh Chaudhry serves as the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the bank.
  • Other Banks' Roles (Incorrect Options):
    • HDFC bank: While it has extensive MSME lending programs and the 'SmartHub Vyapar' app, it did not launch the ‘Evolve’ summit.
    • IDFC FIRST Bank: Known for its focus on retail banking and SME funding, but it is not the host of this specific knowledge series.
    • Federal bank: A major private sector bank based in Kerala that offers digital lending to small businesses but is not associated with the 7th edition of Evolve.

Important Points

  • Digital Transformation for MSMEs: The 7th edition emphasized that digitalization is no longer an option but a necessity for MSMEs to improve operational efficiency and customer reach.
  • Government Initiatives: The summit also highlighted how MSMEs can leverage government schemes like PMEGP (Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme) and Udyam Registration to access collateral-free loans.
  • Export Focus: A key objective of the Axis bank Evolve summit was to educate entrepreneurs on how to tap into Global Value Chains (GVCs), helping India reach its target of $5 trillion economy.
  • Previous Editions: Since its inception in 2014, the Evolve summit has reached over 15,000 MSMEs across 30 cities in India, providing them with educational content and networking opportunities.

questions.text: <!-- x-tinymce/html -->Which of the following coins are called as small coins?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Coins up to 50 paise.

Key Points

  • Small coins in India refer to coins with denominations lower than one rupee. These coins are typically used for smaller transactions in daily life.
  • The classification of "small coins" includes coins up to 50 paise, as per the guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Hence, coins of denominations like 10 paise, 20 paise, 25 paise, and 50 paise fall under this category.
  • Coins above 50 paise, such as ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, etc., are categorized as "Rupee coins" and not small coins.
  • Small coins were traditionally made from materials like nickel, copper, or aluminum to keep production costs low, and they were widely circulated before higher-value transactions became more common.
  • With advancements in technology and shifts in consumer behavior, the use of coins of smaller denominations (like 10 paise and 25 paise) has diminished, leading to their gradual phase-out by the RBI.

Additional Information

  • Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Guidelines:
    • The RBI is the central authority responsible for issuing and managing currency and coins in India.
    • In June 2011, the RBI withdrew coins of denominations below 50 paise (i.e., 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, and 25 paise) from circulation, citing reduced demand and higher production costs.
    • Currently, coins of 50 paise and above are considered legal tender in India.
  • Legal Tender:
    • The term "legal tender" means coins or currency that must be accepted if offered in payment of a debt.
    • Coins of 50 paise are the smallest denomination still classified as legal tender in India, while lower denominations like 25 paise are no longer valid.
  • Material Composition of Small Coins:
    • Coins of lower denominations were historically made from materials like aluminum, nickel, and copper.
    • The lightweight and cost-effective production of these coins made them suitable for widespread circulation during earlier decades.
  • Phasing Out of Small Coins:
    • The usage of small coins has reduced significantly over the years due to inflation and the increasing preference for digital transactions.
    • For instance, coins below 50 paise were demonetized in 2011, and their circulation was completely ceased.

Important Points

  • Historical Context:
    • India began issuing its own coins in 1950 after gaining independence, with denominations ranging from 1 paise to higher values.
    • The decimalization of the Indian currency in 1957 further standardized the coinage system, introducing smaller denominations like 1 paise and 2 paise coins.
  • 50 Paise Coin:
    • The 50 paise coin holds historical significance as the highest denomination among small coins and is still considered legal tender.
    • It is widely recognized for its role in facilitating smaller financial transactions in local markets.
  • Digital Transactions and Decline in Coin Usage:
    • With the rise of digital payment platforms like UPI, mobile wallets, and online banking, the reliance on physical coins, especially small denominations, has decreased significantly.
    • This shift has contributed to the gradual phase-out of coins below 50 paise.

questions.text: Which among the following is the oldest Public Sector Bank of India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Allahabad Bank.

Key Points

  • Allahabad Bank was founded on 24 April 1865, making it the oldest public sector bank in India.
  • The bank was established in Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh, during the British Raj.
  • In 2020, Allahabad Bank merged with Indian Bank as part of a consolidation plan by the Government of India.
  • Before its merger, Allahabad Bank had a wide presence with over 3,000 branches across India.

Additional Information

  • Public Sector Banks (PSBs):
    • These are banks where the majority stake is held by the Government of India.
    • PSBs play a crucial role in the financial inclusion and economic development of the country.
  • Bank Mergers in India:
    • In recent years, the Indian government has merged several PSBs to create larger and stronger banks.
    • The mergers aim to improve efficiency, reduce the number of non-performing assets (NPAs), and enhance the overall financial stability of the banking sector.
  • Indian Bank:
    • Founded in 1907 and headquartered in Chennai, Tamil Nadu.
    • After the merger with Allahabad Bank, Indian Bank became one of the largest public sector banks in India.
  • Banking Sector Reforms:
    • The Indian government has undertaken various reforms to strengthen the banking sector, including the introduction of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) and recapitalization plans.
    • These reforms aim to address issues such as NPAs, improve governance, and ensure better management of resources.

  • Its board put the United Bank of India in voluntary liquidation on 21 March 1874, and Alliance Bank commenced operations two days later

questions.text: When did Government of India announced Demonetisation
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is November 8, 2016. 

Key PointsMeaning of Demonetization: 

  • Demonetization is the act of invalidating or withdrawing the legal tender status of a particular currency.
  • It involves the discontinuation of certain denominations of banknotes, rendering them no longer accepted as a medium of exchange.
  • Demonetization is usually implemented by a government or central bank as a measure to address issues such as black money, counterfeit currency, corruption, and the funding of illegal activities.
  • The process typically involves announcing a specific deadline for the affected currency to be exchanged or deposited in banks, after which it loses its value.
  • Demonetization can have significant effects on the economy and society, including disruptions in cash-based transactions, a shift towards digital payments, and efforts to identify unaccounted wealth.

Important Points

  •  On November 8, 2016, the Government of India made a significant announcement of demonetization.
  • This move involved the sudden invalidation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes as legal tender, with the aim of addressing issues like black money, corruption, counterfeit currency, and illegal activities.
  • The decision sparked widespread reactions and had a profound impact on the economy and society.
  •  Additionally, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched to encourage financial inclusion and provide avenues for individuals to deposit their old currency within a specified time frame.

questions.text: Small Industries Development Bank of India Act was passed in which of the following years?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 1989.Key Points 

  • SIDBI is the principal development financial institution for promotion, financing, and development of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector in India.
  • It was established on April 2, 1990, under an Act of Parliament 1989.
  • The headquarters of the SIDBI is located in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.
  • It aims to facilitate and strengthen credit flow to MSMEs and address both financial and developmental gaps in the MSME eco-system across the country.
  • It coordinates the functions of institutions engaged in similar activities.

  • Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry and Small Industries Development Bank of India, SIDBI has signed an MoU to engage SIDBI as the implementation agency for PM Street Vendor’s AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi).
  • The Ministry had launched the PM SVANidhi on 1st June 2020 for providing affordable Working Capital loan to street vendors.
  • This scheme targets to benefit over 50 lakh Street Vendors.

questions.text: In which year was the RBI formally inaugurated?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is '1935'.

Key Points

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central bank and regulatory body responsible for the regulation of the Indian banking system.
  • It was set up on the basis of the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission.
  • RBI was formally inaugurated on April 1, 1935.
  • It commenced its operations in accordance with the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
  • Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor of the Bank. 
  • The Central Office of the RBI was established in Calcutta (now Kolkata) but was moved to Bombay (now Mumbai) in 1937.
  • The Bank, which was originally set up as a shareholder's bank, was nationalized in 1949.
